- When sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to underreact — increase forecast slightly above recent mean or avoid early sharp declines.
- When sentiment is bearish (≤0.33) and price is trending down, model often overcorrects downward — avoid excessive drops; consider slight upward bias to prevent premature bottoming.
- After a sharp price spike, model frequently overestimates continuation — reduce forecast momentum in next 3–5 days unless sentiment confirms bullish momentum.
- If sentiment shifts from bearish to bullish mid-period, model often lags — adjust forecast upward by 1–2% of recent range to capture sentiment reversal faster.
- Model tends to underestimate mean reversion in 30-day horizon — if sentiment is neutral or mixed, add 0.5–1.5% upward bias to account for volatility clustering.
- When sentiment is high and price is near support, model often forecasts a breakout — if true outcome shows consolidation or reversal, reduce forecast by 0.5–1.5% to avoid over-optimism.
- If sentiment is low and price is near resistance, model often forecasts a drop — if true outcome shows sideways or slight bounce, increase forecast by 0.5–1.5% to avoid pessimism.
